name: Invoice Capture and Coding
title: Invoice Capture and Coding
answer: Invoice capture and coding covers the path a supplier invoice takes from arrival to a posted, coded entry in the accounts payable ledger. It spans intake from email, supplier portals, scan batches and electronic formats, extraction of header and line level data, matching against purchase orders and receipts, and assignment of general ledger codes, cost centres and tax treatment. The work sits between accounts payable operations, procurement and the accounting function, and it is judged on whether the resulting entry is correct and supported rather than on how quickly a document was read.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Invoice capture and coding covers the path a supplier invoice takes from arrival to a posted, coded entry in the accounts payable ledger. It spans intake from email, supplier portals, scan batches and electronic formats, extraction of header and line level data, matching against purchase orders and receipts, and assignment of general ledger codes, cost centres and tax treatment. The work sits between accounts payable operations, procurement and the accounting function, and it is judged on whether the resulting entry is correct and supported rather than on how quickly a document was read.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack usually begins with a capture layer that accepts PDFs, scanned images, email attachments and structured feeds such as EDI or e-invoicing formats. Optical character recognition and document layout models turn pages into text and coordinates, and a classification step decides whether a document is an invoice, a credit note or something else. Extracted fields are held in a queue or staging table, then pushed into an ERP or accounting system through an API or a batch import, with the original document image stored alongside the record so the entry can be traced back to its source.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Extraction combines template rules for known suppliers with learned models for unfamiliar layouts, and confidence scores are attached to each field. Coding is often driven by supplier history, purchase order lines, item descriptions and a chart of accounts mapping, with rules for tax codes, currency and cost centre defaults. Most implementations route low confidence documents or mismatched totals to a human reviewer, and the corrections made there are fed back to improve the mapping. Three way matching against purchase order and goods receipt remains the main control before an invoice is approved for payment.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are duplicate payment, altered bank details, fabricated invoices and mis coded spend that distorts reporting. Controls include duplicate detection on supplier, invoice number and amount, segregation between capture and approval, and validation of supplier master data changes. Audit trails must show what the system extracted, what a person changed and when, because tax authorities and external auditors may ask for the original document and the coding rationale. Data protection rules apply to any personal data on an invoice, and retention schedules determine how long images and extracted records are kept.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Adoption is moving toward continuous, touchless processing for routine, low risk invoices, with human attention concentrated on exceptions and new suppliers. Structured e-invoicing mandates in several jurisdictions are shifting the intake problem from reading paper to validating structured data, which changes where the effort sits. The open questions are how much autonomy to grant coding decisions, how to evidence that autonomy to auditors, and how to keep supplier master data clean enough that automation does not simply scale an existing error.
